SEO translation: how to rank in other languages

October 26, 2023
Translation services | Globalisation | International Development

SEO translation is the process of translating your website content so that it ranks in search engines in another language, as well as reading well to the people who find it.

A standard translation changes the words.

SEO translation also changes the keywords, the headings, the meta titles and descriptions and the page structure, so each market sees content that matches the way its customers actually search.

If you sell to customers in France, Germany, Spain or beyond, this is what turns a translated website into a source of enquiries.

What SEO translation involves

SEO translation combines three skills: professional translation, keyword research and search engine optimisation.

A literal translation of your English keywords rarely works, because people in other countries often search with different words, and sometimes with different intent.

The most popular search term in your market may not be the closest translation of your English keyword.

Keyword research in each language

The work starts by defining the keywords for each target market.

Linguists and SEO specialists use keyword research tools and your own Google Search Console data to find the terms people really use, including regional variations in wording.

The search volume for those terms decides which ones become your focus keywords for each page.

Translation that follows search intent

Search intent describes what a user wants when they type a query: information, a comparison or a purchase.

A product page needs persuasive, transactional copy, while a blog post needs clear, helpful information.

The translator then writes the page to match that intent, with the target keyword in the right places and the text still sounding natural.

Metadata, URLs and internal links

SEO translation covers more than the visible text.

Page titles, meta descriptions, headings, image alt text, URL slugs and internal link anchors all need translating and optimising, because search engines and users read them.

How search engines treat translated websites

Google publishes clear guidance for multilingual sites.

It recommends a separate URL for each language version, one language per page, and hreflang annotations so that search results link to the correct language version.

Google also notes that localised versions of a page are only considered duplicates if the main content stays untranslated.

In practice, this means your translated pages need genuinely translated content, a clean technical set-up and a structure that search engines can follow.

The website translation service covers the linguistic side, and your developers or SEO team can handle the technical side with the translated content you receive.

The benefits of SEO translation

  • Visibility in new markets: your pages can appear for searches in other languages, not only in English.
  • Qualified traffic: visitors arrive using terms that match what you sell, so they are more likely to enquire or buy.
  • Credibility: native-quality copy shows you understand the local market and culture.
  • Better user experience: localised content, currency and examples make pages easier to read and act on.

These benefits matter most for e-commerce, travel, software and professional services, where customers compare options online before they get in touch.

If you run an online shop, the Spanish retail and e-commerce and German e-commerce pages show how this works for specific markets.

Why quality still matters

SEO knowledge cannot make up for a weak translation.

Poor translations damage how your brand is perceived and confuse the visitors you worked to attract.

Keyword-stuffed text reads badly and rarely converts, even when it ranks.

That is why SEO translation works best when a native-speaking translator who understands your industry writes the copy and a second linguist reviews it.

Machine translation can give you a draft, but it does not know your target keywords, your tone of voice or the preferences of a local market.

How to choose an SEO translation company

Look for a provider that can answer these questions clearly.

  • Who does the keyword research, and which tools and data do they use?
  • Are the translators native speakers who specialise in your sector?
  • Does the service include metadata, headings, URLs and alt text?
  • How is quality checked before delivery?
  • Can the team work with your CMS, your developers and your SEO agency?

Be wary of any provider that promises a particular ranking, because no one controls what search engines display.

Work with BeTranslated on your multilingual SEO

BeTranslated works with native-speaking linguists across a wide range of industries, including marketing.

BeTranslated can translate and optimise your website, product pages and blog content, and offers multilingual SEO support if you want a wider strategy beyond the translation itself.

Every project is quoted per project, based on your languages, the volume of content and the level of optimisation you need.

To get started, request a free, no-obligation quote.

Frequently asked questions

What is SEO translation?

It is the translation of web content with search optimisation built in. The translator uses researched keywords for the target market, adapts titles and descriptions and writes copy that matches local search intent.

How is SEO translation different from standard translation?

Standard translation focuses on conveying the meaning of the source text. SEO translation also considers the keywords people search for in the target language, the page structure and metadata, so the page can rank as well as read well.

Do you need to translate meta titles and URLs?

Yes. Meta titles, descriptions, headings and URL slugs are all visible to search engines and users, so translating and optimising them helps each language version appear in the right results. Google also recommends a separate URL for each language version.

Can machine translation be used for SEO?

It can produce a first draft, but it does not research keywords or judge search intent. A human linguist should review and adapt the text before you publish it, especially on pages that drive enquiries or sales.

How long does it take for translated pages to rank?

It varies with competition, the age of your site and the quality of your technical set-up, so no provider can give an exact date. Most businesses measure progress over months using impressions, rankings and enquiries in each market.
